about: Introduction to University Mathematics (MATH40001) is a 5-ECTS core module that fills the first four weeks of Term 1 on Imperial's Mathematics BSc (about 24 lectures and 16 classes). It moves students from school-style calculation to the precise definitions and rigorous proofs used throughout the degree. The handbook names the topic areas as sets, functions and relations, proof strategies, the natural, rational and real numbers, and elementary vectors and geometry; this pack splits those areas into seven topics. The 2026–27 handbook lists group coursework (20%), a portfolio of small quizzes and written coursework (10%) and a final exam in week 4 (70%); weightings can change from year to year, so check the current handbook. The module is pass/fail only and does not count towards the year total; the pass mark is 50% rather than 40%, and several attempts at the final assessment are allowed.

notes.body:
Almost every object in university mathematics is built from sets, so the module starts by making the language of sets precise. The aim is not new facts but exact definitions and the habit of proving set identities properly.

Basic language
- A set is a collection of objects, its elements. x ∈ A means x is an element of A.
- Sets are equal when they have exactly the same elements: order and repetition do not matter, so {1, 2, 2} = {2, 1}.
- Set-builder notation: {x ∈ ℝ : x² < 4} is the interval (−2, 2).
- A ⊆ B (A is a subset of B) means every element of A is in B. A = B exactly when A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A.
- The empty set ∅ has no elements and is a subset of every set. Note that ∅ and {∅} are different: the second has one element.

Operations
- Union: A ∪ B = {x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B} ("or" is inclusive).
- Intersection: A ∩ B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B}. A and B are disjoint if A ∩ B = ∅.
- Difference: A ∖ B = {x ∈ A : x ∉ B}.
- Symmetric difference: A Δ B = (A ∖ B) ∪ (B ∖ A), the elements in exactly one of the sets.
- Complement (relative to a universal set U): Aᶜ = U ∖ A.
- Example: A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5} give A ∩ B = {3, 4}, A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, A ∖ B = {1, 2} and A Δ B = {1, 2, 5}.

Power sets and products
- The power set P(A) is the set of all subsets of A. If A has n elements, P(A) has 2ⁿ elements, because each element is either in or out of a subset.
- P(∅) = {∅} has one element, and P(P(∅)) = {∅, {∅}} has two.
- The Cartesian product A × B = {(a, b) : a ∈ A, b ∈ B} is the set of ordered pairs. If |A| = m and |B| = n, then |A × B| = mn.

Proving set identities: double inclusion
To prove X = Y, take an arbitrary x ∈ X and show x ∈ Y, then do the reverse. For example, De Morgan's law A ∖ (B ∪ C) = (A ∖ B) ∩ (A ∖ C):
- If x ∈ A ∖ (B ∪ C), then x ∈ A and x ∉ B ∪ C, so x ∉ B and x ∉ C. Hence x ∈ A ∖ B and x ∈ A ∖ C.
- Conversely, if x is in both A ∖ B and A ∖ C, then x ∈ A, x ∉ B and x ∉ C, so x ∉ B ∪ C.
The companion law is A ∖ (B ∩ C) = (A ∖ B) ∪ (A ∖ C). With complements: (B ∪ C)ᶜ = Bᶜ ∩ Cᶜ and (B ∩ C)ᶜ = Bᶜ ∪ Cᶜ.

Other useful identities
- Distributive laws: A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C) and A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C).
- A ⊆ B if and only if A ∩ B = A, if and only if A ∪ B = B.
- Venn diagrams are good for guessing identities and finding counterexamples, but they do not count as proofs.

Why care about precision?
Not every description defines a set: Russell's paradox (the "set of all sets that are not members of themselves") shows that unrestricted collection leads to contradiction. In practice, always build sets as subsets of a set you already have.

Exam tips: in set proofs, start with "Let x ∈ …" and keep every step as a statement about x; translate ∪, ∩ and ∖ into "or", "and" and "and not". To show two sets are different, give one explicit element in one but not the other.

A function is the basic way to compare and transport structure between sets. At university a function is not just a formula: the domain and codomain are part of its definition.

Definition
A function f: A → B assigns to each element a of the domain A exactly one element f(a) of the codomain B.
- The image (range) of f is f(A) = {f(a) : a ∈ A}, which may be smaller than B.
- For S ⊆ B, the preimage is f⁻¹(S) = {a ∈ A : f(a) ∈ S}. This makes sense even when f has no inverse.
- Two functions are equal when they have the same domain, the same codomain and the same value at every point.

Injective, surjective, bijective
- Injective (one-to-one): f(a₁) = f(a₂) implies a₁ = a₂. Different inputs give different outputs.
- Surjective (onto): for every b ∈ B there is some a ∈ A with f(a) = b. The image is all of B.
- Bijective: both injective and surjective.

How to prove them
- Injective: assume f(a₁) = f(a₂) and deduce a₁ = a₂.
- Surjective: take an arbitrary b ∈ B, construct an a, and check that it lies in A and that f(a) = b.
- Not injective: exhibit a₁ ≠ a₂ with f(a₁) = f(a₂). Not surjective: exhibit b with no preimage.

Examples where the sets matter
- x ↦ x², ℝ → ℝ, is neither injective (f(−1) = f(1)) nor surjective (−1 is not hit).
- The same rule from [0, ∞) to [0, ∞) is a bijection.
- n ↦ 2n + 1, ℤ → ℤ, is injective but not surjective (no even number is hit), whereas x ↦ 2x + 1, ℝ → ℝ, is a bijection with inverse y ↦ (y − 1)/2.

Composition and inverses
- (g ∘ f)(a) = g(f(a)), defined when the codomain of f is the domain of g. Composition is associative.
- If f and g are injective, so is g ∘ f; similarly for surjective and bijective.
- If g ∘ f is injective, then f is injective (but g need not be). If g ∘ f is surjective, then g is surjective (but f need not be). Example: f: {1} → {1, 2} and the constant map g: {1, 2} → {1}; then g ∘ f is a bijection, though g is not injective and f is not surjective.
- f has an inverse f⁻¹: B → A with f⁻¹ ∘ f = id_A and f ∘ f⁻¹ = id_B if and only if f is a bijection.
- To find an inverse, solve y = f(x) for x and check the answer lies in the domain. For f(x) = (2x + 1)/(x − 3) from ℝ ∖ {3} to ℝ ∖ {2}, the inverse is y ↦ (3y + 1)/(y − 2).

Counting (finite sets, |A| = m, |B| = n)
- There are nᵐ functions A → B.
- There are n(n − 1)…(n − m + 1) injections if m ≤ n, and none if m > n (the pigeonhole principle).
- From a 3-element set to a 2-element set there are 2³ = 8 functions, of which 6 are surjective (all except the two constant maps).
- From a 3-element set to a 5-element set there are 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 injections.

Size of infinite sets
Two sets have the same cardinality if there is a bijection between them. For example, n ↦ 2n is a bijection from ℤ to the even integers, so a set can have the same size as a proper subset of itself.

Exam tips: always state the domain and codomain before answering injectivity or surjectivity questions; when proving surjectivity, show the element you construct really lies in the domain.

Relations formalise the idea of comparing elements, and equivalence relations formalise "the same in the respect we care about". They are how mathematicians build new objects such as the integers mod n and the rational numbers.

Relations
A relation R on a set A is a subset of A × A; we write a R b when (a, b) ∈ R. Important properties:
- Reflexive: a R a for every a ∈ A.
- Symmetric: a R b implies b R a.
- Transitive: a R b and b R c imply a R c.
- Antisymmetric: a R b and b R a imply a = b.

Examples
- ≤ on ℝ is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive (a partial order, in fact a total order), but not symmetric.
- "Divides" on the positive integers and ⊆ on subsets of a set are also partial orders.
- x ~ y if |x − y| < 1 on ℝ is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive: 0 ~ 0.6 and 0.6 ~ 1.2, but 0 is not related to 1.2.
- = on any set is the simplest equivalence relation.

Equivalence relations
An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. The equivalence class of a is [a] = {x ∈ A : x ~ a}.
Key facts:
- a ∈ [a], so classes are non-empty and cover A.
- [a] = [b] if and only if a ~ b.
- Two classes are either equal or disjoint.
So the equivalence classes form a partition of A: a collection of non-empty, pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is A. Conversely, every partition comes from exactly one equivalence relation ("in the same block"). This bijection means, for example, that there are 5 equivalence relations on {1, 2, 3}, one for each partition: {1}{2}{3}; {1, 2}{3}; {1, 3}{2}; {2, 3}{1}; and {1, 2, 3}.

Congruence modulo n
For a fixed n ≥ 1, define a ≡ b (mod n) if n divides a − b.
- Reflexive: n divides 0.
- Symmetric: if a − b = kn then b − a = (−k)n.
- Transitive: if a − b = kn and b − c = ln then a − c = (k + l)n.
There are n classes, [0], [1], …, [n − 1], and the set of classes is ℤₙ. Addition [a] + [b] = [a + b] and multiplication [a][b] = [ab] are well defined: they do not depend on which representatives a, b are chosen.

Well-definedness
Whenever you define an operation on equivalence classes using representatives, you must check that equivalent representatives give equivalent answers. For example, "[a] ↦ a" is not a well-defined function from ℤ₃ to ℤ, because [1] = [4] but 1 ≠ 4.

Constructing ℚ
On pairs (a, b) with a, b ∈ ℤ and b ≠ 0, define (a, b) ~ (c, d) if ad = bc. This is an equivalence relation, and the class of (a, b) is what we mean by the fraction a/b; this is why 1/2 = 2/4. Transitivity uses b, d ≠ 0 to cancel: from ad = bc and cf = de we get d(af − be) = 0, so af = be.

Exam tips: check the three properties one by one with general elements, and for a failure give a specific counterexample. When describing equivalence classes, say how many there are and give a representative of each.

notes.h: Logic and strategies for writing proofs
notes.body:
The module's main goal is to move from calculating answers to proving statements. A proof is a chain of justified statements leading from hypotheses to a conclusion, written in sentences that a reader can check.

Statements and connectives
- "P and Q" (P ∧ Q), "P or Q" (P ∨ Q, inclusive), "not P" (¬P).
- "P implies Q" (P ⇒ Q) is false only when P is true and Q is false. So a false hypothesis makes an implication vacuously true.
- The converse of P ⇒ Q is Q ⇒ P, which is a different statement. The contrapositive ¬Q ⇒ ¬P is logically equivalent to P ⇒ Q.
- "P if and only if Q" (P ⇔ Q) means both P ⇒ Q and Q ⇒ P, and is usually proved in two parts.

Quantifiers and negation
- ∀ means "for all" and ∃ means "there exists". Order matters: "∀x ∃y with y > x" is true in ℝ, but "∃y ∀x with y > x" is false.
- Negation swaps the quantifiers and negates the inner statement: ¬(∀x P(x)) is ∃x ¬P(x), and ¬(∃x P(x)) is ∀x ¬P(x).
- ¬(P ⇒ Q) is P ∧ ¬Q. So the negation of "∀ε > 0 ∃δ > 0 ∀x (|x| < δ ⇒ |f(x)| < ε)" is "∃ε > 0 ∀δ > 0 ∃x (|x| < δ and |f(x)| ≥ ε)". Note that "ε > 0" is a restriction on the quantifier, so it is not negated.

Proof strategies
- Direct proof: assume P and deduce Q. Example: if m and n are odd, write m = 2a + 1 and n = 2b + 1; then mn = 2(2ab + a + b) + 1 is odd.
- Contrapositive: to show "n² even ⇒ n even", prove "n odd ⇒ n² odd". If n = 2k + 1 then n² = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1.
- Contradiction: assume the statement is false and deduce something impossible. Euclid's proof that there are infinitely many primes assumes a finite list p₁, …, pₖ and considers N = p₁p₂…pₖ + 1. N > 1, so N has a prime factor, but N leaves remainder 1 on division by each pᵢ, so that factor is not in the list.
- Cases: split into exhaustive cases (n even or odd; x ≥ 0 or x < 0) and prove each. For example, n³ − n = (n − 1)n(n + 1) is a product of three consecutive integers, so it is divisible by 2 and by 3, and hence by 6.
- Counterexample: one example disproves a "for all" statement. n² + n + 41 is prime for n = 0, 1, …, 39, but at n = 40 it equals 1681 = 41².
- Existence and uniqueness: to show "there is exactly one", show that one exists and that any two must be equal.

Writing proofs well
- Say what you assume and what you are proving ("Suppose…", "We show that…").
- Define every variable you introduce, with its type (for example "let k ∈ ℤ").
- Use words such as "so", "hence" and "since" to justify each step; do not just list equations.
- Never start from the statement to be proved and work towards something true. That shows only the converse.

Exam tips: before writing, identify the hypothesis, the conclusion and which strategy fits; for a negation, move the ¬ inwards step by step; and read your proof back as a sceptical reader would.

The natural numbers are where proof by induction lives. The module treats ℕ carefully, because its defining property, that there is no infinite descent, is exactly what makes induction valid. Conventions differ on whether 0 ∈ ℕ, so check your lecture notes and always state your starting value.

Principle of mathematical induction
Let P(n) be a statement for each integer n ≥ n₀. If
- (base case) P(n₀) is true, and
- (inductive step) for every n ≥ n₀, P(n) implies P(n + 1),
then P(n) is true for every n ≥ n₀.

Strong induction
If P(n₀) holds and, for every n ≥ n₀, the truth of P(n₀), …, P(n) together implies P(n + 1), then P(n) holds for all n ≥ n₀. This is equivalent to ordinary induction, but more convenient when P(n + 1) depends on earlier cases.

Well-ordering principle
Every non-empty subset of ℕ has a least element. This is equivalent to induction, and it underlies "minimal counterexample" proofs: if a statement failed somewhere, there would be a smallest failure, and you show that is impossible.

Worked examples
- Sum of squares: 1² + 2² + … + n² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 for n ≥ 1. Base case n = 1: both sides are 1. Inductive step: assuming it for n,
  n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 + (n + 1)² = (n + 1)[n(2n + 1) + 6(n + 1)]/6 = (n + 1)(2n² + 7n + 6)/6 = (n + 1)(n + 2)(2n + 3)/6,
  which is the formula for n + 1.
- Divisibility: 3 divides 4ⁿ − 1 for all n ≥ 0. Base case: 4⁰ − 1 = 0. Step: 4ⁿ⁺¹ − 1 = 4(4ⁿ − 1) + 3, and both terms are multiples of 3.
- Inequality: 2ⁿ > n² for all n ≥ 5. Base case: 32 > 25. Step: if 2ⁿ > n² with n ≥ 5, then 2ⁿ⁺¹ > 2n² = n² + n² ≥ n² + 5n > n² + 2n + 1 = (n + 1)². Note that the statement is true at n = 1 but false for n = 2, 3 and 4 (4 = 4, 8 < 9, 16 = 16), so the base case must be chosen with care.
- Strong induction: every integer n ≥ 2 is a product of primes. If n + 1 is prime, we are done. Otherwise n + 1 = ab with 2 ≤ a, b ≤ n, and by the hypothesis both a and b are products of primes, so n + 1 is too.
- Sum of odd numbers: 1 + 3 + … + (2n − 1) = n².

Recursive definitions
Induction also defines things: n! by 0! = 1 and (n + 1)! = (n + 1) × n!, or sequences such as aₙ₊₁ = 2aₙ + 1 with a₀ = 0, for which induction proves aₙ = 2ⁿ − 1.

Common errors
- Checking a few cases is not a proof.
- The inductive step must work for every n ≥ n₀. The false "all horses are the same colour" argument breaks exactly at the step from 1 to 2, where the two overlapping groups do not share a horse.
- Do not assume P(n + 1) and work backwards; start from P(n) and reach P(n + 1).

Exam tips: label "Base case", "Inductive hypothesis" and "Inductive step", say exactly where the hypothesis is used, and finish with a concluding sentence that names the principle of induction.

notes.h: Rationals and reals: irrationality and completeness
notes.body:
The module asks what distinguishes the real numbers from the rationals. The answer, completeness, is the foundation of the Analysis module that follows.

Rational numbers
- ℚ = {a/b : a, b ∈ ℤ, b ≠ 0}, where a/b = c/d means ad = bc (formally, fractions are equivalence classes of pairs).
- ℚ is closed under +, −, × and division by non-zero numbers, and it is ordered.
- A real number is rational exactly when its decimal expansion terminates or eventually repeats. For example 0.272727… = 27/99 = 3/11.

Irrational numbers
Theorem: √2 is irrational.
Proof by contradiction: suppose √2 = p/q with p, q integers, q ≠ 0 and the fraction in lowest terms. Then p² = 2q², so p² is even, so p is even (by the contrapositive argument: odd squares are odd). Write p = 2r. Then 4r² = 2q², so q² = 2r² and q is even. So p and q are both even, which contradicts lowest terms.
- The same argument shows √3 is irrational, using the fact that if 3 divides n² then 3 divides n (since 3 is prime, or by checking n ≡ 1 or 2 mod 3 gives n² ≡ 1 mod 3).
- If r is rational and x is irrational, then r + x is irrational, and so is rx when r ≠ 0. For example √3 + 1 is irrational.
- Products and sums of irrationals can be rational: √2 × √8 = 4, and √2 + (−√2) = 0.

Bounds, supremum and infimum
Let S be a non-empty subset of ℝ.
- u is an upper bound of S if s ≤ u for every s ∈ S.
- The supremum sup S is the least upper bound: it is an upper bound, and no smaller number is. Equivalently, for every ε > 0 there is s ∈ S with s > sup S − ε.
- The infimum inf S is the greatest lower bound.
- A maximum is a supremum that belongs to S. The supremum may exist without being attained: for S = {1 − 1/n : n ≥ 1}, sup S = 1 but 1 ∉ S, while inf S = min S = 0.

The completeness axiom
Every non-empty subset of ℝ that is bounded above has a supremum in ℝ.
- ℚ fails this. The set {x ∈ ℚ : x² < 2} is bounded above, but it has no least upper bound in ℚ, because its supremum in ℝ is √2.
- Completeness is what makes ℝ "have no gaps". It is used to prove that bounded monotonic sequences converge and that continuous functions satisfy the intermediate value theorem.

Consequences
- Archimedean property: for every real x there is a natural number n > x. Equivalently, for every ε > 0 there is n with 1/n < ε.
- Density of ℚ: between any two real numbers a < b there is a rational number. Choose n with 1/n < b − a; then some m/n lies in (a, b).
- Density of the irrationals: between any two reals there is also an irrational number, for instance a rational plus a small rational multiple of √2.
- 0.999… = 1, because the partial sums 1 − 10⁻ⁿ have supremum 1.

Exam tips: in irrationality proofs, state the lowest-terms assumption and say exactly where the contradiction arises. When finding a supremum, prove both parts: that it is an upper bound and that nothing smaller is.

The final strand revisits vectors from school, now with precise definitions and proofs. It prepares directly for the linear algebra module.

Vectors in ℝ² and ℝ³
- A vector is an ordered list of real numbers, such as a = (a₁, a₂, a₃), added and scaled componentwise.
- The length (norm) is |a| = √(a₁² + a₂² + a₃²). A unit vector has length 1, and a/|a| is the unit vector in the direction of a ≠ 0.
- The vector from point P to point Q is q − p, where p and q are the position vectors.

The dot (scalar) product
a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃.
- It is symmetric and linear in each argument, and a · a = |a|².
- a · b = |a||b| cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors. So non-zero vectors are perpendicular exactly when a · b = 0.
- Cauchy–Schwarz inequality: |a · b| ≤ |a||b|, with equality exactly when one vector is a multiple of the other. Proof: the case b = 0 is trivial; for b ≠ 0, |a − tb|² ≥ 0 for every real t is a quadratic in t that never goes negative, so its discriminant is at most 0.
- Triangle inequality: |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|, which follows from Cauchy–Schwarz.
- Example: a = (1, 2, 2) and b = (3, 0, 4) give a · b = 11, |a| = 3, |b| = 5, so cos θ = 11/15 and θ ≈ 42.8°.

The cross (vector) product, in ℝ³ only
a × b = (a₂b₃ − a₃b₂, a₃b₁ − a₁b₃, a₁b₂ − a₂b₁).
- a × b is perpendicular to both a and b, with direction given by the right-hand rule.
- |a × b| = |a||b| sin θ, the area of the parallelogram spanned by a and b.
- b × a = −(a × b), and a × a = 0. The cross product is not associative.
- Example: (1, 2, 2) × (3, 0, 4) = (8, 2, −6). Check: its dot product with each vector is 0, and |a × b|² = 104 = |a|²|b|² − (a · b)² = 225 − 121.
- Scalar triple product: a · (b × c) is the signed volume of the parallelepiped spanned by a, b and c, and equals the determinant of the 3 × 3 matrix with rows a, b and c. It is zero exactly when the three vectors are coplanar.

Lines
- Vector form: r = a + λd, with a point a, a direction d ≠ 0 and λ ∈ ℝ.
- Two lines in ℝ³ may intersect, be parallel, or be skew (neither).

Planes
- Normal form: n · r = d, or n₁x + n₂y + n₃z = d, where n is a normal vector.
- A normal to the plane through points P, Q and R is (q − p) × (r − p).
- Example: the plane through (1, 0, 0), (0, 2, 0) and (0, 0, 3) is 6x + 3y + 2z = 6.
- The distance from point p₀ to the plane n · r = d is |n · p₀ − d|/|n|. From (1, 1, 1) to 6x + 3y + 2z = 6 it is |11 − 6|/7 = 5/7, since |n| = √49 = 7.
- To intersect a line with a plane, substitute r = a + λd into the plane equation and solve for λ. For r = (1, 1, 0) + λ(1, −1, 2) and the plane above, 9 + 7λ = 6, so λ = −3/7 and the point is (4/7, 10/7, −6/7).

Exam tips: check cross products by dotting with both original vectors, include |n| when computing distances, and always state whether a line and plane meet, are parallel, or the line lies in the plane.

cards.f: How to prove two sets are equal
cards.b: Double inclusion: show X ⊆ Y and Y ⊆ X, each by taking an arbitrary element.
(A ∖ B) ∪ (B ∖ A): the elements in exactly one of A and B.
A ∖ (B ∪ C) = (A ∖ B) ∩ (A ∖ C) and A ∖ (B ∩ C) = (A ∖ B) ∪ (A ∖ C).

cards.f: Size of the power set of an n-element set
cards.b: 2ⁿ, since each element is either in or out of a subset.
∅ has no elements; {∅} has exactly one element, namely ∅. P(∅) = {∅}.
The set of ordered pairs (a, b) with a ∈ A, b ∈ B; it has |A||B| elements for finite sets.
A rule assigning to every a ∈ A exactly one f(a) ∈ B; the domain and codomain are part of the definition.
f(a₁) = f(a₂) implies a₁ = a₂.
For every b ∈ B there is a ∈ A with f(a) = b.

cards.f: When does f have a two-sided inverse?
cards.b: Exactly when f is a bijection.

cards.f: If g ∘ f is injective, what follows?
cards.b: f is injective (g need not be).

cards.f: If g ∘ f is surjective, what follows?
cards.b: g is surjective (f need not be).

cards.b: {a ∈ A : f(a) ∈ S}; defined for any function, even one with no inverse.
A relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
{x : x ~ a}. Classes are non-empty, cover the set, and any two are equal or disjoint.
A collection of non-empty, pairwise disjoint subsets of A whose union is A.
5, one for each partition of the set.
A relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive, e.g. ≤ on ℝ or ⊆ on subsets.
n divides a − b. An equivalence relation on ℤ with n classes [0], …, [n − 1].
Its result does not depend on which representatives of the classes are used.
¬Q ⇒ ¬P, which is logically equivalent to P ⇒ Q.
Q ⇒ P. It is not equivalent to P ⇒ Q.
P ∧ ¬Q (P holds and Q fails).
Only when P is true and Q is false.

cards.f: Euclid's idea for infinitely many primes
cards.b: Given primes p₁, …, pₖ, the number p₁…pₖ + 1 has a prime factor not in the list.

cards.f: Counterexample to 'n² + n + 41 is always prime'

cards.b: If P(n₀) holds and P(n) ⇒ P(n + 1) for all n ≥ n₀, then P(n) holds for all n ≥ n₀.

cards.f: Smallest N with 2ⁿ > n² for all n ≥ N
cards.b: N = 5 (it fails at n = 2, 3, 4).
4ⁿ⁺¹ − 1 = 4(4ⁿ − 1) + 3, a sum of multiples of 3.

questions.q: Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5}. What is the symmetric difference A Δ B?
questions.why: A Δ B = (A ∖ B) ∪ (B ∖ A) = {1, 2} ∪ {5} = {1, 2, 5}. {3, 4} is the intersection, the elements in both sets. {1, 2} is only A ∖ B and leaves out the element 5 that is in B but not A. {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} is the union, which wrongly keeps the shared elements 3 and 4.

questions.q: How many elements does P(P(∅)) have?
questions.why: P(∅) = {∅} has one element, so its power set has 2¹ = 2 elements: ∅ and {∅}. The answer 1 is the size of P(∅), so the power set was taken only once. The answer 0 assumes the power set of the empty set is empty, forgetting that ∅ is a subset of itself. The answer 4 treats P(∅) as having two elements, giving 2².

questions.q: Prove that for any sets A, B and C, A ∖ (B ∪ C) = (A ∖ B) ∩ (A ∖ C).
markScheme: States the method of double inclusion
Takes x ∈ A ∖ (B ∪ C) and deduces x ∈ A, x ∉ B, x ∉ C
Concludes x ∈ (A ∖ B) ∩ (A ∖ C)
Reverse inclusion: x ∈ A ∖ B and x ∈ A ∖ C gives x ∈ A and x ∉ B ∪ C
Clear concluding sentence
questions.modelAnswer: We show each side is a subset of the other. Let x ∈ A ∖ (B ∪ C). Then x ∈ A and x ∉ B ∪ C. Since x is not in the union, x ∉ B and x ∉ C. So x ∈ A ∖ B and x ∈ A ∖ C, that is x ∈ (A ∖ B) ∩ (A ∖ C). Conversely, let x ∈ (A ∖ B) ∩ (A ∖ C). Then x ∈ A, x ∉ B and x ∉ C. Since x is in neither B nor C, x ∉ B ∪ C, so x ∈ A ∖ (B ∪ C). Both inclusions hold, so the sets are equal.

questions.q: Let f: ℤ → ℤ be f(n) = 2n + 1. Which is true?
options: f is injective but not surjective
f is a bijection
f is surjective but not injective
f is neither injective nor surjective
questions.why: If 2m + 1 = 2n + 1 then m = n, so f is injective, but no even integer is of the form 2n + 1, so f is not surjective. 'Bijection' is true for x ↦ 2x + 1 on ℝ, where (y − 1)/2 is always available, but over ℤ it is not an integer for even y. 'Surjective but not injective' swaps the two definitions. 'Neither' correctly sees that f is not surjective but wrongly concludes that injectivity fails too.

questions.q: For functions f: A → B and g: B → C, suppose g ∘ f is injective. What must be true?
options: f is injective
g is injective
Both f and g are injective
f is surjective
questions.why: If f(a₁) = f(a₂) then g(f(a₁)) = g(f(a₂)), so a₁ = a₂ by injectivity of g ∘ f. Hence f is injective. g need not be: take f: {1} → {1, 2} and the constant map g: {1, 2} → {1}; then g ∘ f is injective but g is not. 'Both' fails for the same example. 'f is surjective' mixes this up with the result for surjective composites, which says g is surjective; the same f is not surjective.

questions.q: Let f: ℝ ∖ {3} → ℝ ∖ {2} be f(x) = (2x + 1)/(x − 3). Show that f is well defined and bijective, and find f⁻¹.
markScheme: Shows f(x) ≠ 2: (2x + 1)/(x − 3) = 2 leads to 1 = −6, impossible
Solves y = (2x + 1)/(x − 3) for x: x = (3y + 1)/(y − 2)
Checks this x is defined for y ≠ 2 and is not 3 (3y + 1 = 3y − 6 is impossible)
Concludes surjective, and injective because the solution is unique (or direct check)
States f⁻¹(y) = (3y + 1)/(y − 2)
questions.modelAnswer: Well defined: x ≠ 3, so the formula makes sense, and if (2x + 1)/(x − 3) = 2 then 2x + 1 = 2x − 6, which is impossible, so f(x) ∈ ℝ ∖ {2}. Now let y ≠ 2 and solve y = (2x + 1)/(x − 3): yx − 3y = 2x + 1, so x(y − 2) = 3y + 1 and x = (3y + 1)/(y − 2). This x is defined because y ≠ 2, and x ≠ 3 because (3y + 1)/(y − 2) = 3 would give 3y + 1 = 3y − 6. So every y has exactly one preimage: f is surjective, and the uniqueness of the solution shows it is injective. Hence f is a bijection with f⁻¹(y) = (3y + 1)/(y − 2).

questions.q: On ℝ, define x ~ y if |x − y| < 1. Which properties does ~ have?
options: Reflexive and symmetric, but not transitive
It is an equivalence relation
Reflexive and transitive, but not symmetric
Symmetric and transitive, but not reflexive
questions.why: |x − x| = 0 < 1 gives reflexivity and |x − y| = |y − x| gives symmetry, but 0 ~ 0.6 and 0.6 ~ 1.2 while |0 − 1.2| = 1.2, so transitivity fails. Calling it an equivalence relation skips the transitivity check. The relation is defined by a symmetric expression, so it cannot fail symmetry. Reflexivity holds because every |x − x| is 0.

questions.q: How many different equivalence relations are there on the set {1, 2, 3}?
questions.why: Equivalence relations correspond to partitions: {1}{2}{3}, the three ways to pair two elements and leave one alone, and {1, 2, 3}, giving 1 + 3 + 1 = 5. The answer 3 counts only the possible numbers of classes (1, 2 or 3), not the different partitions. 6 is 3!, the number of orderings, which has nothing to do with partitions. 8 is 2³, the number of subsets of the set.

questions.q: Define a ~ b on ℤ if 3 divides a − b. Prove that ~ is an equivalence relation and describe its equivalence classes.
markScheme: Reflexive: a − a = 0 = 3 × 0
Symmetric: a − b = 3k gives b − a = 3(−k)
Transitive: a − b = 3k, b − c = 3l gives a − c = 3(k + l)
Three classes [0], [1], [2], by the remainder on division by 3
Notes the classes partition ℤ
questions.modelAnswer: Reflexive: a − a = 0 = 3 × 0, so a ~ a. Symmetric: if a − b = 3k with k ∈ ℤ, then b − a = 3(−k), so b ~ a. Transitive: if a − b = 3k and b − c = 3l, then a − c = (a − b) + (b − c) = 3(k + l), so a ~ c. Hence ~ is an equivalence relation. By the division algorithm every integer is 3q, 3q + 1 or 3q + 2, and two integers are related exactly when they leave the same remainder. So there are three classes: [0] = {…, −3, 0, 3, …}, [1] = {…, −2, 1, 4, …} and [2] = {…, −1, 2, 5, …}. They partition ℤ.

questions.q: What is the negation of '∀ε > 0 ∃δ > 0 ∀x (|x| < δ ⇒ |f(x)| < ε)'?
questions.why: Each quantifier flips (∀ ↔ ∃) and the inner implication P ⇒ Q becomes P ∧ ¬Q. The version that still starts '∀ε ∃δ ∀x' negates only the final inequality and leaves the quantifiers unchanged. The version with |x| ≥ δ negates the hypothesis of the implication as well, but ¬(P ⇒ Q) keeps P. The version with ε ≤ 0 and δ ≤ 0 negates the restrictions on the quantifiers, which only say which ε and δ are being quantified over.

questions.q: To prove 'if n² is even then n is even' by contrapositive, which statement do you prove?
options: If n is odd then n² is odd
If n is even then n² is even
If n² is odd then n is odd
If n is odd then n² is even
questions.why: The contrapositive of P ⇒ Q is ¬Q ⇒ ¬P: here 'n not even ⇒ n² not even', that is 'n odd ⇒ n² odd'. 'If n is even then n² is even' is the converse, which is a different statement. 'If n² is odd then n is odd' is the inverse (¬P ⇒ ¬Q), which is equivalent to the converse, not the original. 'If n is odd then n² is even' swaps the two parts correctly but forgets to negate 'n² is even', and it is in fact false (3² = 9).

questions.q: Prove that there are infinitely many prime numbers.
markScheme: Assumes for contradiction that the primes are exactly p₁, …, pₖ
Defines N = p₁p₂…pₖ + 1
Notes N > 1 so N has a prime factor p
Shows p is none of the pᵢ, since each pᵢ leaves remainder 1 when dividing N
States the contradiction and conclusion
questions.modelAnswer: Suppose, for contradiction, that there are only finitely many primes, p₁, p₂, …, pₖ. Let N = p₁p₂…pₖ + 1. Then N > 1, so N has at least one prime factor p (every integer greater than 1 is a product of primes). Since p is prime, p = pᵢ for some i. But pᵢ divides p₁p₂…pₖ, so if it also divided N it would divide N − p₁…pₖ = 1, which is impossible. This contradiction shows there are infinitely many primes. (Note that N itself need not be prime: 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 11 × 13 + 1 = 30031 = 59 × 509.)

questions.q: What is the smallest N such that 2ⁿ > n² for every integer n ≥ N?
options: There is no such N, since n² eventually overtakes 2ⁿ
questions.why: 2ⁿ > n² holds at n = 1 (2 > 1) but fails at n = 2 (4 = 4), n = 3 (8 < 9) and n = 4 (16 = 16); it holds at n = 5 (32 > 25) and induction shows it holds from then on. N = 1 checks only the first case and ignores the failures at 2, 3 and 4. N = 4 forgets the inequality is strict, since 16 = 16. Claiming there is no such N gets the growth rates backwards: exponentials eventually beat any polynomial.

questions.q: In a proof by induction that 1² + 2² + … + n² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6, what must the inductive step show?
options: Assuming the formula for n + 1, it also holds for n
The formula holds for n = 1, 2 and 3
questions.why: Assuming the formula for n, adding the next term (n + 1)² must give the formula with n replaced by n + 1. The version adding n² adds the wrong term: the n-th square is already in the sum. Deducing the case n from the case n + 1 runs the argument backwards and proves nothing about larger n. Checking n = 1, 2, 3 is a set of base cases, not an inductive step, and examples alone are never a proof.

questions.q: Prove by induction that 3 divides 4ⁿ − 1 for every integer n ≥ 0.
markScheme: Base case n = 0: 4⁰ − 1 = 0, divisible by 3
Inductive hypothesis: 4ⁿ − 1 = 3k for some integer k
Rewrites 4ⁿ⁺¹ − 1 = 4(4ⁿ − 1) + 3
Concludes 4ⁿ⁺¹ − 1 = 3(4k + 1)
Concluding statement citing induction
questions.modelAnswer: Let P(n) be '3 divides 4ⁿ − 1'. Base case: 4⁰ − 1 = 0 = 3 × 0, so P(0) holds. Inductive step: suppose P(n) holds for some n ≥ 0, so 4ⁿ − 1 = 3k with k ∈ ℤ. Then 4ⁿ⁺¹ − 1 = 4 × 4ⁿ − 4 + 3 = 4(4ⁿ − 1) + 3 = 12k + 3 = 3(4k + 1), so P(n + 1) holds. By the principle of induction, 3 divides 4ⁿ − 1 for all n ≥ 0.

questions.q: Let S = {1 − 1/n : n a positive integer}. Which statement is correct?
options: sup S = 1, and S has no maximum
max S = 1
sup S = 0
S has no supremum, because it is infinite
questions.why: Every element is less than 1, and for any ε > 0 choosing n > 1/ε gives 1 − 1/n > 1 − ε, so 1 is the least upper bound; it is never reached because 1/n > 0. 'max S = 1' assumes the supremum must belong to S. 0 is the infimum (and minimum, at n = 1), not the supremum. Being infinite does not matter: by completeness any non-empty set bounded above has a supremum.

questions.q: Which of these numbers is irrational?
options: 0.272727… (with 27 recurring)
questions.why: √3 is irrational and adding the rational 1 keeps it irrational. √2 × √8 = √16 = 4, so a product of irrationals can be rational. A recurring decimal is rational: 0.272727… = 27/99 = 3/11. √(9/4) = 3/2, because a square root sign does not by itself make a number irrational.

questions.q: Prove that √3 is irrational.
markScheme: Assumes √3 = p/q in lowest terms with q ≠ 0
Derives p² = 3q²
Justifies 3 | p² ⇒ 3 | p (prime property or residues mod 3)
Writes p = 3r to get q² = 3r², so 3 | q
Contradiction with lowest terms stated
questions.modelAnswer: Suppose √3 is rational, say √3 = p/q with p, q integers, q ≠ 0 and the fraction in lowest terms. Squaring gives p² = 3q², so 3 divides p². Then 3 divides p: otherwise p ≡ 1 or 2 (mod 3), and then p² ≡ 1 (mod 3). Write p = 3r. Then 9r² = 3q², so q² = 3r², and by the same argument 3 divides q. So 3 divides both p and q, contradicting lowest terms. Hence √3 is irrational.

questions.why: Using (a₂b₃ − a₃b₂, a₃b₁ − a₁b₃, a₁b₂ − a₂b₁) gives (8 − 0, 6 − 4, 0 − 6) = (8, 2, −6), and this is perpendicular to both vectors. (8, −2, −6) comes from the determinant expansion with the minus sign on the middle cofactor forgotten. (−8, −2, 6) is b × a, the product taken in the wrong order. (3, 0, 8) multiplies the components pairwise, which is not a vector product.

questions.q: What is the distance from the point (1, 1, 1) to the plane 6x + 3y + 2z = 6?
questions.why: The distance is |n · p₀ − d|/|n| = |6 + 3 + 2 − 6|/√(36 + 9 + 4) = 5/7. The answer 5 forgets to divide by |n| = 7. The answer 11/7 forgets to subtract d = 6. The answer 5/49 divides by |n|² instead of |n|.

questions.q: Find the equation of the plane Π through (1, 0, 0), (0, 2, 0) and (0, 0, 3). Then find where the line r = (1, 1, 0) + λ(1, −1, 2) meets Π.
markScheme: Finds two direction vectors in the plane, e.g. (−1, 2, 0) and (−1, 0, 3)
Normal by cross product: (6, 3, 2)
Plane 6x + 3y + 2z = 6 (checked on the three points)
Substitutes the line: 6(1 + λ) + 3(1 − λ) + 2(2λ) = 6, giving λ = −3/7
Intersection point (4/7, 10/7, −6/7)
questions.modelAnswer: Two vectors in the plane are (0, 2, 0) − (1, 0, 0) = (−1, 2, 0) and (0, 0, 3) − (1, 0, 0) = (−1, 0, 3). Their cross product is (2 × 3 − 0 × 0, 0 × (−1) − (−1) × 3, (−1) × 0 − 2 × (−1)) = (6, 3, 2). So Π is 6x + 3y + 2z = d, and (1, 0, 0) gives d = 6. Each of the three points satisfies 6x + 3y + 2z = 6. On the line, x = 1 + λ, y = 1 − λ and z = 2λ, so 6 + 6λ + 3 − 3λ + 4λ = 6, which gives 9 + 7λ = 6 and λ = −3/7. The point is (4/7, 10/7, −6/7); check: 24/7 + 30/7 − 12/7 = 6.

questions.q: Let X = {(a, b) : a, b ∈ ℤ, b ≠ 0} and define (a, b) ~ (c, d) if ad = bc. (a) Prove that ~ is an equivalence relation on X. [8] (b) Explain why the equivalence classes can be identified with rational numbers, and give two different elements of the class of (1, 2). [3] (c) Define [(a, b)] + [(c, d)] = [(ad + bc, bd)]. Explain why bd ≠ 0 and prove that this addition is well defined. [6] (d) Show that the map ℤ → X/~ given by n ↦ [(n, 1)] is injective. [3]
markScheme: (a) Reflexive: ab = ba
(a) Symmetric: ad = bc implies cb = da
(a) Transitive: from ad = bc and cf = de deduce d(af − be) = 0
(a) Uses d ≠ 0 to cancel and conclude af = be
(b) The class of (a, b) is the fraction a/b; e.g. (2, 4) and (−3, −6) are in the class of (1, 2)
(c) bd ≠ 0 because b, d ≠ 0 and ℤ has no zero divisors
(c) Shows (ad + bc)b′d′ = (a′d′ + b′c′)bd using ab′ = a′b and cd′ = c′d
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Reflexive: for (a, b) ∈ X, ab = ba, so (a, b) ~ (a, b).
Symmetric: if (a, b) ~ (c, d) then ad = bc, so cb = da, which says (c, d) ~ (a, b).
Transitive: suppose (a, b) ~ (c, d) and (c, d) ~ (e, f), so ad = bc and cf = de. Multiply the first equation by f: adf = bcf. Using cf = de, the right side is bde. So adf = bde, that is d(af − be) = 0. Since (c, d) ∈ X, d ≠ 0, and an integer product is zero only if a factor is zero, so af − be = 0, that is af = be, and (a, b) ~ (e, f).
Hence ~ is an equivalence relation.

(b) We want a/b = c/d exactly when ad = bc, which is the cross-multiplication rule for fractions. So the class [(a, b)] collects all the pairs that represent the same fraction, and we define the rational number a/b to be that class. For example (2, 4) and (−3, −6) are both in the class of (1, 2), since 1 × 4 = 2 × 2 and 1 × (−6) = 2 × (−3).

(c) Since b ≠ 0 and d ≠ 0, and ℤ has no zero divisors, bd ≠ 0, so (ad + bc, bd) ∈ X.
Well defined: suppose (a, b) ~ (a′, b′) and (c, d) ~ (c′, d′), so ab′ = a′b and cd′ = c′d. We must show (ad + bc, bd) ~ (a′d′ + b′c′, b′d′), that is
(ad + bc)b′d′ = (a′d′ + b′c′)bd.
The left side is (ab′)dd′ + (cd′)bb′ = (a′b)dd′ + (c′d)bb′. The right side is a′d′bd + b′c′bd, which is the same pair of terms. So the class of the sum does not depend on the representatives chosen, and the addition is well defined.

(d) Suppose [(m, 1)] = [(n, 1)]. Then (m, 1) ~ (n, 1), so m × 1 = 1 × n and m = n. Hence the map is injective, and ℤ sits inside ℚ as the classes [(n, 1)], the fractions n/1.

questions.q: (a) Prove by induction that 1² + 2² + … + n² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 for all n ≥ 1. [6] (b) Prove that 2ⁿ > n² for all integers n ≥ 5, and show that 5 cannot be replaced by 4. [6] (c) Use strong induction to prove that every integer n ≥ 2 can be written as a product of primes. [5] (d) The following argument claims that all horses in any group of n ≥ 1 horses are the same colour: 'A group of one horse is clearly one colour. Given n + 1 horses, remove one: the remaining n are the same colour. Remove a different one: those n are the same colour. The two groups overlap, so all n + 1 are the same colour.' Identify precisely where the argument fails. [3]
markScheme: (a) Base case n = 1 checked
(a) Inductive step: adds (n + 1)² and factorises to (n + 1)(n + 2)(2n + 3)/6
(b) Base case 32 > 25 and counterexample 2⁴ = 16 = 4²
(b) Inductive step: 2ⁿ⁺¹ > 2n² ≥ n² + 5n > n² + 2n + 1, using n ≥ 5
(c) Strong hypothesis for all 2 ≤ k ≤ n; cases n + 1 prime or n + 1 = ab with 2 ≤ a, b ≤ n
(c) Combines prime factorisations of a and b
(d) The step from n = 1 to n = 2 fails because the two groups of size 1 do not overlap
Clear structure and conclusion in each part
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Let P(n) be the statement 1² + … + n² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6.
Base case: for n = 1 the left side is 1 and the right side is 1 × 2 × 3/6 = 1.
Inductive step: assume P(n) for some n ≥ 1. Then
1² + … + n² + (n + 1)² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 + (n + 1)²
= (n + 1)[n(2n + 1) + 6(n + 1)]/6
= (n + 1)(2n² + 7n + 6)/6
= (n + 1)(n + 2)(2n + 3)/6,
which is P(n + 1). By induction, P(n) holds for all n ≥ 1.

(b) Base case: 2⁵ = 32 > 25 = 5².
Inductive step: suppose 2ⁿ > n² for some n ≥ 5. Then 2ⁿ⁺¹ = 2 × 2ⁿ > 2n² = n² + n × n ≥ n² + 5n (since n ≥ 5) = n² + 2n + 3n > n² + 2n + 1 = (n + 1)². So 2ⁿ⁺¹ > (n + 1)², and by induction the inequality holds for all n ≥ 5.
5 cannot be replaced by 4, because at n = 4, 2⁴ = 16 = 4², so the strict inequality fails.

(c) Let P(n) be the statement 'n is a product of primes' (a prime counts as a product of one prime).
Base case: 2 is prime.
Inductive step: suppose P(k) holds for every k with 2 ≤ k ≤ n, and consider n + 1. If n + 1 is prime, we are done. Otherwise n + 1 = ab with 1 < a, b < n + 1, so 2 ≤ a, b ≤ n. By the strong inductive hypothesis, a and b are both products of primes, so their product n + 1 is too. By strong induction, P(n) holds for every n ≥ 2.
Ordinary induction would not work directly, because a and b are not n.

(d) The base case is true and the step works whenever the two groups of n horses share at least one horse, which happens when n ≥ 2. The step from n = 1 to n = 2 fails: with two horses, removing one leaves {horse 1} and removing the other leaves {horse 2}. These groups do not overlap, so nothing links the two colours. Since the inductive step must hold for every n ≥ 1, the argument is invalid.
